420.bp: This paper studies a very small-looking decision that stands in for many web and marketplace problems: one opportunity appears now, later opportunities are unknown, and saying no cannot be undone. The story is hiring a single secretary from candidates who arrive one by one in random order, but the same shape appears whenever a system must accept or reject a streamed offer before seeing the rest of the stream. The company wants the hired candidate to have high value, yet it never sees the full list at decision time. Classical work asks for a multiplicative comparison with the best candidate that hindsight would choose, producing the familiar 1/e law. This paper asks a different practical question: if every candidate value is scaled between 0 and 1, how many value points can the online rule lose in the worst case compared with hindsight? That absolute loss is regret, and the paper builds selection rules around lowering it.
420.wh: The hard part is that waiting and acting are both dangerous for opposite reasons. If the company hires early, it may discover later that much stronger candidates were still coming. If it waits too long, the best candidate may already have passed and cannot be recalled. The random arrival order helps, because early candidates are a sample of what the stream might contain, but it does not reveal future values. The older competitive-ratio view also hides a practical tension. A ratio can make sense when values vary wildly, but when every value is normalized between 0 and 1, a company may care more about the absolute number of value points it leaves on the table. Losing 0.6 of a normalized value is a very different promise from losing 0.25. The paper is hard because it changes the yardstick, then must design and prove policies for the new yardstick.
420.naive: A smart beginner might copy the classical rule: ignore an initial fraction of candidates, remember the best value seen there, then hire the first later candidate who beats that remembered value. This is natural because the early sample gives a rough standard without spending the hiring slot. It fails under the regret yardstick because the rule was tuned for a ratio guarantee, not for a bounded absolute gap. The abstract states that the 1/e law has regret 1 - 1/e, about 0.632, even though values lie between 0 and 1. That means the rule can still be far from the hindsight best in the worst case. A second naive rule, using one fixed cutoff value, also fails because the right standard should change as time runs out.
420.ap: The paper's central move is to judge online selection by additive regret and then use pricing curves as the decision language. A pricing curve can be understood as a time-dependent acceptance price: at each point in the arrival process, the current candidate must be valuable enough to be worth spending the one hiring opportunity. Early in the stream, the price can be stricter because many candidates remain. Later, the price can fall because the option to wait is becoming less useful. The paper shows that this family can guarantee regret at most 1/4, and that this is the best possible guarantee within that class. It also studies a narrower best-only version, where the rule depends on the best candidate seen so far, and shows an even smaller guarantee of at most 0.190, with a lower bound of 0.171. The point is not just a new rule, but a new measurement of what good online hiring means.
420.mech: The input is a sequence of candidate values, each revealed only when that candidate arrives. The order is assumed uniformly random, so the position of a candidate in the stream is not chosen by an adversary after seeing the policy. The policy watches the stream one value at a time. At each arrival, it has the current time position, the values already seen, and the fact that only one hire can be made. A pricing-curve policy turns that state into an acceptance threshold, like a reservation price. If the current candidate clears the relevant price, the policy hires and stops. If not, it rejects the candidate forever and moves to the next arrival. After the whole thought experiment is complete, analysis compares the expected value earned by the policy with the value of the best candidate that hindsight could have selected from the full sequence. The regret is the worst-case additive gap between those two quantities, after values are normalized to the 0 to 1 range. The authors then prove upper bounds for policy classes: no pricing-curve algorithm in their class needs lose more than 0.25, best-only pricing curves can get to 0.190, and no policy of any kind can push the guarantee below 0.152. The mechanism therefore has two layers: the online rule for acting, and the proof that the rule's worst possible absolute loss is bounded.
420.math: The main mathematical idea is online decision-making under incomplete information. The chooser sees only the past and present, while the comparison point is an all-seeing hindsight chooser that knows every value. That mismatch creates regret: a number measuring how much value the limited-information rule gives up. Here regret is additive, meaning it is a direct subtraction between hindsight value and expected policy value, not a ratio. Normalizing values between 0 and 1 makes that subtraction meaningful across instances, because the largest possible value scale is fixed. Probability enters through the uniformly random arrival order. The values themselves can be difficult, but their positions are random, so an early sample has usable information about the stream without revealing everything. A pricing curve is a mathematical function from time, and possibly past observations, to an acceptance standard. It encodes the tradeoff between selectiveness and scarcity of remaining chances. Worst-case analysis asks for a guarantee that holds against the hardest value sequence allowed by the setup, not just an average easy case. Tightness and lower bounds are also central: saying 0.25 is tight within pricing curves means the analysis is not merely failing to find a better curve; within that rule family, a stronger promise is impossible. The general 0.152 lower bound says even unrestricted policies face a fundamental information limit.
420.dots: This paper belongs with online selection algorithms, but it also connects to several recurring conference ideas. It is a ranking problem compressed into a single irreversible choice: many candidates have values, yet the system can keep only one. It is also a sequential decision problem, like regret-based bandit and routing papers in the repo, because the policy must act before all evidence arrives and is judged by the loss from not knowing enough soon enough. The connection to optimization is the design of a decision rule that minimizes a clearly defined bad outcome, here worst-case additive regret. Unlike recommendation or retrieval papers that can show several items and learn from repeated user feedback, this setting has one slot and no recall. Unlike graph or language-model papers, there is no rich structure among items; the structure is temporal. That simplicity is useful: it isolates the cost of making an irreversible online decision under a random order.
420.ww: The pricing-curve idea works better than the naive classical rule because it matches the new loss measurement. Under additive regret, the question is not only whether the policy captures a constant fraction of the best value. It is how far, in normalized value points, the expected hire can fall below hindsight. A curve can express the changing value of waiting. At the beginning, rejecting a merely decent candidate is less costly because many chances remain. Near the end, the same rejection is more dangerous because the stream is nearly exhausted. By moving the acceptance standard over time, the policy balances two mistakes: spending the hire too cheaply and preserving the hire until it becomes useless. The best-only variant adds a grounded reference point from the observed stream: the best value so far tells the policy something about what counts as strong in this instance. The regret proofs matter because this intuition could otherwise be accidental. The stated upper and lower bounds show where the improvement is real, where a policy class has reached its limit, and where no online rule can beat the information barrier.
420.po: The payoff is a sharper guarantee for one-shot online selection when values are bounded. The classical 1/e law has regret about 0.632 under this additive view, while pricing curves guarantee at most 0.25, and best-only pricing curves guarantee at most 0.190. The paper also gives lower bounds, including 0.171 for the best-only class and 0.152 for all policies, so the result maps both what the proposed rules can achieve and what no rule can achieve. Practically, it gives designers of streamed selection rules a clearer promise: not just a fraction of hindsight, but a maximum absolute value gap under the model.
420.limits: The claims depend on the formal secretary setting in the abstract. Candidates must arrive in uniformly random order, the company must hire only one, decisions must be irrevocable, and values must be normalized between 0 and 1 for the additive regret numbers to mean what they say. Real hiring or marketplace selection may have correlated arrival order, strategic candidates, multiple hires, interviews that reveal noisy rather than exact values, or legal and fairness constraints not represented by a single value. The abstract reports theoretical guarantees for pricing-curve classes and lower bounds, but it does not show deployment evidence, user costs of false rejection, or how to choose among the other objectives mentioned at the end.

421.bp: The paper starts from a practical security problem in machine learning: the model is trained from examples, and an attacker can corrupt some examples by changing their labels. A picture, text item, or record that should teach the system class A is instead marked as class B. The model then learns from poisoned instruction. The important claim is that the harm is not spread evenly across all classes. Some class pairs are naturally easier to mix up before any attack happens. If the system already has trouble separating those two classes, a flipped label between them gives the attacker a much stronger handle. This matters because a defense that treats every class as equally exposed wastes effort on sturdy boundaries and may leave the fragile ones underprotected. The paper asks what makes one class pair fragile, explains it through class separability, and then builds a defense aimed at the pairs most likely to be damaged.
421.wh: The hard part is that a wrong label is not just a wrong entry in a spreadsheet. During training, each example helps shape how the model divides the world into classes. If two classes are far apart in the evidence the model uses, a few swapped labels look suspicious because they conflict with many clean examples. If two classes are already close, the same swapped labels look more believable. The model can absorb the poison as if it were a normal ambiguous case. That creates unequal vulnerability: the attacker gets more damage by flipping labels between naturally confusable classes than between clearly different classes. A uniform defense misses this structure. It may harden all boundaries a little while failing to widen the exact boundary that is easiest to bend. The abstract also points to a measurement difficulty: susceptibility is governed by underlying separability, not only by the attack recipe or defense name.
421.naive: A smart beginner might defend against label flipping by cleaning labels one at a time, adding more training data, or using one general anti-poisoning rule across all classes. That is reasonable because the attack seems to be about corrupted labels, so the first instinct is to find bad labels or make the model less sensitive to any single example. The failure is that the attack's effect depends on where the flip happens. A cat-to-truck flip and a cat-to-wildcat flip do not carry the same force if the model already sees cats and wildcats as similar. A global rule treats both flips as equally dangerous. It can spend protection on class pairs that were not vulnerable and still leave the closest class pairs easy to confuse.
421.ap: The paper's core move is to make vulnerability a property of class pairs rather than a property of the whole model. It says: look at a source class and a target class, measure how separated they are in the model's internal description of examples, and expect weaker separation to mean greater damage from flipped labels. The abstract calls this standardized separation, which means the distance between the classes is judged relative to how spread out or noisy the classes are, not as a raw distance alone. From that diagnosis, the defense becomes targeted. Confusability-Aware Contrastive Learning, or CACL, uses comparison-based training: examples from the most vulnerable class pairs are pressured to move farther apart in the model's learned feature space, meaning the numeric description the model uses before deciding a label. The goal is not generic toughness; it is to widen the boundaries that an attacker can most easily exploit.
421.mech: The mechanism can be read as a pipeline. The input is a labeled training set with several classes and the possibility that some labels have been flipped from a source class to a target class. First, the model represents each example by learned features, which are numbers summarizing what the model thinks is useful for telling classes apart. Second, the method examines class pairs rather than only overall accuracy. For each pair, it asks how easy it is to confuse them: are their feature clouds well separated, or do they sit near each other relative to their own spread? Third, the theoretical analysis connects this measured closeness to vulnerability, arguing that lower standardized separation fundamentally creates more exposure to label flipping. Fourth, CACL uses that exposure map to choose the most vulnerable class pairs as special training targets. For those pairs, it applies a comparison pressure: examples that belong to different vulnerable classes should be pulled away from each other in the learned feature space, while examples that belong together should remain organized enough for classification. Fifth, after this training pressure changes the representation, the classifier has a cleaner boundary between the classes that were previously easiest to poison. The output is still an ordinary classifier over classes, but its internal geometry has been reshaped so flipped labels between confusable classes are less able to drag the decision boundary into the wrong place.
421.math: The main mathematical idea is separability: how clearly two groups can be divided using the evidence the model has learned to keep. Imagine each example as a point in a map made by the model. A class is then a cloud of points, not a single dot. Two clouds can have centers that are far apart, but if each cloud is very spread out, they may still overlap. That is why standardized separation matters. It compares distance with internal spread, asking whether the gap is large enough relative to the noise and variation inside the classes. The second idea is vulnerability as a pairwise quantity. Instead of asking whether the model is generally secure, the analysis asks how a flip from one specific class into another changes learning when those two classes are close. The third idea is comparison-based learning, named in the abstract as contrastive learning. In plain terms, training creates paired pressures: things that should not be confused are pushed apart, and useful within-class organization is preserved. The tradeoff is separation versus distortion. If the method pushes too broadly, it could damage useful shared structure. CACL therefore focuses the pressure on the pairs whose low separation makes them attack-prone.
421.dots: This paper sits in the adversarial robustness theme, but it also connects to two recurring conference ideas in the repo: similarity and learning from examples. The similarity concept says that models often decide by arranging examples in a learned map and measuring nearness. This paper shows the security risk of that same map: if two classes are near, poison travels more easily between them. The self-supervised and contrastive family uses constructed comparisons to decide what should be close and what should be far. CACL uses that family logic defensively, turning pairwise comparison into a way to repair fragile class boundaries. It also neighbors broader security work in the privacy and security family, where the shared question is not only whether a model works on clean data, but what useful signal can be trusted when an attacker strategically changes what the system sees. Here the attack surface is the training label itself.
421.ww: The method should help because it targets the actual path by which label flipping causes harm. A flipped label is most persuasive when it can be blended into an already ambiguous boundary. If the model's feature map places two classes close together, then poisoned examples between them do not look like extreme outliers; they look like additional evidence that the boundary should move. Increasing separation for those class pairs changes the cost of the attack. The attacker can still flip labels, but the flipped examples now conflict more strongly with the model's learned organization. Clean examples from each class form more distinct regions, so a few wrong labels have less ability to make the target class borrow the source class's evidence. This is why the paper's diagnosis and defense fit together. The theory identifies low standardized separation as the weakness, and CACL spends training pressure exactly on widening those low-separation gaps rather than applying an equal amount of defense everywhere.
421.po: The payoff is a more precise way to understand and defend against label flipping. The paper does not merely say attacks hurt accuracy; it explains why some classes are hurt more than others. Experiments validate the strong link between class separability and vulnerability, according to the abstract, and show that CACL significantly reduces the attack's impact while giving stronger protection to the most susceptible classes. Practically, this means a defender can inspect which class pairs are intrinsically confusable and harden those boundaries first. That is a more useful security plan than treating the model as one uniform object with one uniform level of risk.
421.limits: The claims depend on the model's learned feature space being a faithful place to measure class confusability. If those features are poorly learned, biased, or changed by a different training setup, the measured vulnerable pairs may be misleading. The defense also assumes that pushing vulnerable class pairs farther apart does not remove useful shared structure needed for normal accuracy. The abstract reports extensive experiments, but it does not specify from this input which datasets, attack budgets, model types, or label-noise patterns were tested. It also does not prove that CACL handles adaptive attackers who know the defense and choose flips to exploit new weaknesses.

422.bp: Large Web AI systems are useful only after they have been trained on many examples, but that training consumes time, electricity, and money. Dataset distillation tries to reduce that burden by replacing a full training set with a much smaller synthetic one: not the original photographs or labels, but carefully made examples that teach a model nearly the same lesson. The practical promise is that a lab or company could train downstream models cheaply without repeatedly using the large source data. AMID focuses on the point where that promise often breaks. A tiny dataset made while working with one model family, such as a convolutional network, can quietly learn that family's habits. When a different family, such as a vision transformer, studies the same synthetic set, the lesson does not transfer well. The paper's real target is therefore reusable compression: one distilled dataset that saves energy because it can serve many architectures instead of being rebuilt for each one.
422.wh: The hard part is that a synthetic training set must do two opposite things at once. It must keep the useful visual class knowledge from the original data, because otherwise later models will not learn the task. At the same time, it must drop traces of the particular source architecture used during distillation. Those traces are tempting because they help the source model perform well during the distillation process, so an ordinary method may reward them without noticing. A convolutional network and a vision transformer do not look at images in the same way: one has built-in local image habits, while the other is designed around different comparison patterns across image pieces. If the distilled images become tuned to one habit, they become less useful to the other. The result is a hidden cost: each new architecture needs its own distillation run, which undercuts the energy and carbon savings that motivated dataset distillation in the first place.
422.naive: A smart beginner would take a large image dataset, choose one strong source model, and adjust a small set of synthetic images until training on those images makes that source model behave as if it had seen the full dataset. This seems reasonable because the source model gives concrete feedback: if it learns the classes well, the distilled set looks successful. The failure is that the source model is also a biased judge. It rewards synthetic patterns that fit its own architecture, not necessarily patterns that teach any model. The small dataset can become a private cheat sheet for that model family, so a different architecture reads it poorly and cross-model generalization collapses.
422.ap: AMID's central move is to treat model-agnostic dataset distillation as an information-removal problem. The synthetic data should still say plenty about the task, such as which image patterns distinguish CIFAR-10 or Tiny ImageNet classes, but it should say as little as possible about the identity of the distillation model that helped create it. The paper expresses that unwanted clue as mutual information: how much knowing the synthetic data helps someone guess the source architecture. Directly minimizing that quantity is described as intractable, so AMID turns it into a two-player adversarial game. One side learns synthetic data that preserves useful training knowledge. The other side tries to detect which architecture shaped the synthetic data. The synthetic data is improved when it can still train models but makes that architecture detector fail.
422.mech: The input is a large labeled image dataset, a set of candidate model architectures used during distillation, and a budget for a much smaller synthetic dataset. AMID begins like dataset distillation in general: it creates synthetic examples and repeatedly updates them so that training on them preserves knowledge from the full data. The important addition is a second pressure running at the same time. A discriminator-like player receives signals from the synthetic data and tries to predict the specific distillation model identity, for example whether the data was shaped through a CNN or a vision transformer. If that player can guess correctly, the synthetic examples still carry architecture-specific fingerprints. The synthetic-data player is then pushed to erase those fingerprints while keeping the class-teaching signal. This creates a tug of war. One objective asks the synthetic set to remain useful for learning the original task. The opposing objective asks it to forget the source architecture. Over many updates, the synthetic examples are changed until they balance those demands. The output is not a trained model but a compact synthetic dataset intended to be reused: downstream models from diverse CNN and ViT families can train on it without requiring a separate distillation run for each architecture.
422.math: The main mathematical idea is mutual information, which measures how much one thing reduces uncertainty about another. Here the two things are the synthetic dataset and the identity of the architecture used during distillation. If seeing the synthetic examples makes it easy to guess the source architecture, then the examples contain too much architecture-specific information. If seeing them gives little help in that guessing game, then they are closer to model-agnostic. AMID uses this idea as a way to separate useful signal from unwanted bias. The useful signal is class knowledge: image patterns that help distinguish labels and train well on the downstream task. The unwanted signal is source-model identity: details that help only because one architecture has particular built-in habits. Because the exact mutual-information objective is hard to compute directly, the paper turns it into adversarial learning, meaning two objectives push against each other. One player scores architecture identity, while the other changes the synthetic data to lower that score and preserve task performance. The tradeoff is compression versus transferability: the synthetic set must be small enough to save computation, detailed enough to teach the task, and neutral enough not to become a shortcut for one architecture.
422.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of dataset distillation, information measurement, learning from examples, and efficiency. Like other compression papers in the conference, it asks what can be thrown away without losing the lesson the data was meant to teach. Its difference is that the discarded part is not just noise or redundancy, but a source architecture's fingerprint. That connects it to information-bottleneck ideas: keep the information needed for the task and suppress information that creates brittle behavior. It also sits near adversarial robustness work, because the method uses an opponent whose success exposes a weakness in the current representation. In recommendation, retrieval, and graph papers, similar pressure appears when systems must generalize beyond the narrow data source that shaped them. AMID's specific surface is synthetic image data, but the broader conference theme is reusable learning under scarcity: saving energy, training time, and repeated data processing while avoiding shortcuts that fail when the next model or setting changes.
422.ww: AMID should improve over ordinary distillation because it adds a test that the naive method lacks. A standard distilled set can look good when evaluated on the same kind of model that helped create it, so architecture bias remains invisible until transfer fails. AMID makes that bias visible during training by asking an adversary to identify the source architecture. When the adversary succeeds, it gives a concrete signal that the synthetic data is carrying the wrong kind of information. Pushing against that signal discourages features that are merely convenient for CNNs or merely convenient for ViTs, while the knowledge-preservation objective keeps features that actually help solve the image classification task. In plain terms, the method forces the synthetic examples to become less like private notes for one student and more like a reusable lesson plan. The abstract's reported cross-architecture results are consistent with this mechanism: if architecture-specific clues are reduced, then different model families should find more of the same task-relevant evidence in the compact data.
422.po: The payoff is a distilled dataset that can be reused across model families instead of regenerated for each one. The abstract reports experiments on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, with cross-architecture generalization across CNNs and vision transformers, and says AMID reaches state-of-the-art performance in that transfer setting. The practical benefit is not only accuracy; it is avoiding redundant distillation runs. If one compact dataset can train several downstream architectures, then the energy, computation, and CO2 costs of downstream training drop closer to the original green-AI promise of dataset distillation.
422.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The architectures used in the adversarial game must be broad enough to represent the kinds of models that will later use the synthetic data; otherwise the method may erase only the biases it has seen. The task signal must also be separable from architecture identity, because if useful class knowledge and source-model fingerprints are tangled too tightly, removing one may hurt the other. The abstract names CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, so it does not by itself prove the same behavior for larger Web data, non-image domains, or future architectures. It also reports reduced computation and emissions, but the full accounting depends on the cost of running AMID itself.

423.bp: A web search system is not only a tool for finding documents. It is a public allocation system: it decides which sources receive attention, which users receive useful answers, and which interests are quietly pushed down the page. This tutorial starts from that fact. Fairness in information retrieval matters because ranking errors are not evenly harmless. If a search engine repeatedly under-exposes some publishers, communities, viewpoints, or user needs, it can damage the broader web ecosystem, not just one search session. The paper argues that the field has many fairness-aware retrieval methods and measures, but lacks a clean way to organize what kind of fairness each one is talking about. Its central move is to view the web as an economic market. Users demand information, content providers supply it, and the retrieval system acts like a market mechanism that distributes scarce visibility.
423.wh: The hard part is that fairness in retrieval has more than one owner and more than one clock. A result list can be good for a user in the next ten seconds while still harmful to providers over months if it gives the same high-visibility sources most of the traffic. A rule can protect one individual searcher while doing little for system-wide diversity. Another rule can help a class of suppliers while making a specific user's results less useful. Retrieval itself is already complex because it must interpret a query, compare many possible documents, rank them, and evaluate success from partial feedback. Fairness adds another layer: whose welfare is being measured, which side of the market is being protected, and whether the effect is immediate or cumulative. Without a structure, papers can all claim fairness while solving different problems.
423.naive: A smart beginner would try to fix unfair retrieval by adding a simple constraint to the ranking list: show equal numbers from different groups, or make sure every provider receives some exposure. That is tempting because it turns fairness into a countable property. The failure is that counts alone do not say who is being helped or harmed. Equal provider exposure may still give users poor answers for some queries. High user satisfaction may still concentrate traffic on already dominant suppliers. A one-session fix can also create long-term imbalance if repeated rankings train users, advertisers, or publishers to behave differently. The simple rule treats fairness as one knob, while the paper's point is that retrieval fairness has several dimensions at once.
423.ap: The tutorial's core idea is to borrow the organizing language of economics rather than invent a separate fairness vocabulary for every retrieval method. Economics has long studied how markets allocate scarce goods among participants with different goals. The paper maps that lens onto information retrieval: attention and visibility are the scarce goods, users and providers are market participants, and ranking algorithms are allocation mechanisms. It then places fairness algorithms inside an economic cube with three axes. Macro versus micro asks whether the concern is the whole system or an individual actor. Demand versus supply asks whether the fairness question is about users seeking information or providers offering content. Short-term versus long-term asks whether the effect is measured in one interaction or over repeated market behavior. The cube does not solve fairness by itself; it makes the target explicit.
423.mech: The mechanism is a conceptual workflow for sorting fairness-aware retrieval work. The input is an information retrieval setting: a query or user need, a collection of candidate items, providers behind those items, users who consume the ranked results, and algorithms or metrics that claim to improve fairness. First, the tutorial draws parallels between retrieval components and market components. A user resembles the demand side because they are asking for information. A document owner, publisher, seller, or content creator resembles the supply side because they provide material competing for attention. The ranking system resembles the market rule because it decides which suppliers reach which demand. Second, the analysis asks whether a fairness method is aimed at macro or micro outcomes. Macro fairness concerns aggregate health, such as whether a whole class of providers is systematically invisible. Micro fairness concerns treatment of particular users, documents, or suppliers. Third, it asks whether the method protects demand or supply. Demand-side fairness asks whether users receive fair access to useful information. Supply-side fairness asks whether providers receive fair opportunity for exposure. Fourth, it asks whether the method handles short-term or long-term effects. Short-term effects concern one ranked list or session; long-term effects concern feedback loops across many rankings. The output is a placement in the economic cube, plus a clearer way to compare algorithms and real-world retrieval applications.
423.math: The mathematics underneath the tutorial is not one new scoring formula; it is an allocation view of ranking. Allocation means deciding how a limited resource is divided among competing participants. In retrieval, the limited resource is top-rank attention: users mostly inspect the first few results, so early positions have much higher value than later ones. Ranking turns many possible documents into an ordered list, and that order allocates exposure. Fairness then becomes a set of comparisons over that allocation. Macro comparison asks about totals across the whole market: are groups of users or suppliers treated acceptably in aggregate? Micro comparison asks about individual treatment: did this user or provider receive a reasonable outcome? Demand and supply separate two sides of welfare, meaning two kinds of benefit that may not rise together. Short-term and long-term reasoning add time: a fair-looking allocation today can change future data, popularity, incentives, and participation. The economic cube is a three-dimensional taxonomy, a way of classifying points by three independent questions. Its value is that it prevents one number from hiding several tradeoffs: relevance versus exposure, user utility versus provider opportunity, and immediate satisfaction versus ecosystem health.
423.dots: This paper connects retrieval fairness to several recurring conference ideas. It is about ranking because the top of a list controls attention, and attention is the resource being distributed. It is about matching because users and providers must be paired through documents, queries, and results, and a locally good match can still produce a poor overall arrangement. It is about fairness and bias because historical clicks, popularity, and existing visibility can look like neutral evidence while carrying old advantage forward. It also touches long-term system behavior, a theme shared with recommendation papers where repeated exposure shapes future demand. Compared with papers that propose one fair reranker or one fairness metric, this tutorial is meta-level: it asks how to name the target before choosing the method. That makes it connective tissue between information retrieval, responsible web systems, market thinking, and evaluation design.
423.ww: The approach works because economics and retrieval share the same hidden shape: many actors want scarce access to something, and a mechanism decides who gets it. Once search is seen this way, several confusing fairness debates become easier to separate. A method that improves supplier diversity is not automatically the same as a method that improves user-side fairness. A metric that looks good for one ranked page does not automatically capture future market effects. A system-wide improvement can still leave individual actors badly treated. The economic cube forces each method to answer three concrete questions before claiming fairness: which scale, which side, and which time horizon? That does not remove disagreement, but it makes disagreement visible. It also helps researchers find empty parts of the map. If many algorithms cover short-term supply-side exposure but few handle long-term demand-side fairness, the field can see that gap rather than mistaking a busy literature for a complete one.
423.po: The payoff is a structured way to summarize and guide fairness-aware information retrieval research. The abstract says the tutorial applies the economic framework to most fairness algorithms and to many real-world retrieval applications. That buys the field a shared vocabulary: instead of saying only that a method is fair, researchers can say what fairness dimension it addresses. Practitioners can also inspect whether a deployment is protecting users, suppliers, individual cases, whole groups, immediate outcomes, or long-term ecosystem effects. The practical gain is clearer diagnosis of tradeoffs before a ranking rule is built or evaluated.
423.limits: The tutorial depends on the economic analogy being useful for a given retrieval setting. Some web harms may not fit cleanly into market language, especially when speech, safety, identity, or political power matter more than ordinary supply and demand. The cube organizes fairness claims, but it does not choose the correct fairness goal for a platform. It also does not prove that an algorithm placed in one cell will work in deployment. Real systems need reliable measurements of users, providers, exposure, welfare, and time effects. The abstract promises broad application and open directions, but not empirical validation of any particular fairness intervention.

424.bp: Community Notes is trying to solve a very practical problem: a social platform has more questionable posts than any central fact-checking team can examine quickly, so it asks many contributors to write and rate short corrective notes. The system does not merely need many votes. It needs agreement across people who usually see the world differently, because a correction that only one side likes may look like another partisan attack. This paper studies what happens after such a note has already passed the platform's agreement test and becomes visible. That moment matters because visibility changes who notices the note, who feels invited to rate it, and what social pressure surrounds it. Using Community Notes on X, the paper asks whether a displayed helpful note remains helpful or whether the act of showing it creates a new political contest around it.
424.wh: The hard part is that the vote being measured is not a fixed property of the note. A note may look broadly acceptable before display because the early raters are a limited sample of contributors. Once the note appears publicly, many more people see it, and the mix of raters can change. The abstract says display triggers a sharp rise in rating volume and a shift in rating leaning, with different effects for different rater groups. That means the system is trying to measure consensus while also changing the crowd whose consensus is being measured. A helpful status can therefore be unstable for two reasons at once: new attention brings more evidence, and polarized attention brings systematically different evidence. The striking empirical sign is that 30.2% of displayed notes later lose helpful status and disappear.
424.naive: A smart beginner might say: compute whether a note is helpful, show it when it passes, and keep showing it unless its text changes. That treats helpfulness like a stable label, similar to stamping a document as approved. The failure is that Community Notes ratings are part of a living social process. Showing the note can attract people who were not part of the original agreement. If contributors close to the note author add supportive ratings while contributors far from the author add negative ratings, the later vote is not just more of the same evidence. It is a different population reacting after the note has become visible.
424.ap: The paper's central move is to treat display as an event that may disturb the rating system, not just as the endpoint of a successful selection process. It gathers a large history of 437,396 notes and 35 million ratings from more than 580,000 contributors, then compares rating behavior around the time each note first becomes visible. The authors separate contributors by viewpoint similarity to the note authors, so they can ask whether supportive and negative movement comes evenly from the whole crowd or unevenly from aligned and opposed groups. They then connect those post-display shifts to later loss of helpful status. In plain terms, the paper turns note disappearance from a mystery into a measured sequence: display, new rating attention, changed leaning, polarized reaction, and possible removal.
424.mech: The mechanism begins with a note, its author, the ratings it receives, and information about how raters relate to the author's viewpoint. Before the note is displayed, the system has an initial path of ratings that leads to helpful status under the platform's bridging-based rule, which is meant to prefer notes accepted across different viewpoints. The paper then marks the display time as a boundary. On the before side, it measures the previous rating level and leaning. On the after side, it measures whether rating volume jumps and whether ratings become more supportive or more negative. The interrupted time series model is the counting device here: it asks whether the line of behavior changes sharply at the moment of display, rather than continuing the old path. The paper also compares rater groups. Contributors similar to note authors tend to increase supportive ratings, while dissimilar contributors increase negative ratings. Finally, counterfactual analyses ask a plain what-if question: if the post-display polarized ratings, especially from dissimilar raters, had not shifted in that way, would the note still have disappeared? The output is not a new fact-checking rule in the abstract; it is evidence about the rating dynamics that turn displayed notes into unstable notes.
424.math: The main mathematical idea is time-based comparison around an interruption. Imagine watching a store's daily visitors, then noting the day a sign is installed. To decide whether the sign mattered, you compare the path before the sign with the path after it, instead of only comparing two totals. Here the sign is note display, and the measured paths are rating volume and rating leaning. A second idea is group comparison: raters are divided by viewpoint similarity to the note authors, and the paper checks whether the same event moves those groups in different directions. Similarity is used as a way of asking who is politically or socially close enough to read the note as friendly. A third idea is counterfactual reasoning, which means asking what would likely have happened under a different version of the same history. The abstract says these analyses suggest post-display polarization plays a substantial role in note disappearance. The tradeoff is precision versus hidden causes: the models can isolate sharp timing and group patterns, but they still rely on the available rating data to stand in for the social forces behind each vote.
424.dots: This paper sits between misinformation detection, social network behavior, ranking, and causal analysis. It is about misinformation because the object being surfaced is a corrective note. It is about social networks because the correction is judged by people whose viewpoints shape their reactions. It is about ranking because Community Notes must decide which annotations are helpful enough to show and which should disappear. It is also close to causal work because the paper asks whether display itself changes later ratings, rather than simply observing that controversial notes receive mixed ratings. Neighboring conference papers on retrieval and recommendation often ask how to choose a small useful item from a large pool. This paper asks a harder governance version of that question: after the system chooses a note, the choice changes the later evidence used to judge whether the choice was right.
424.ww: The approach works because it aligns the measurement with the actual failure mode. If disappearance were caused only by low-quality writing, then ratings after display would simply reveal a note's weakness. But the abstract reports a more structured pattern: display produces more ratings, rating leaning shifts, and the shifts differ by viewpoint group. That structure is exactly what one would expect if visibility invites people to defend or attack a note according to whether it supports their side. The interrupted time comparison helps because the timing is meaningful. A sudden change at display is harder to explain as ordinary slow drift than a gradual change would be. Separating similar and dissimilar raters also matters because total vote counts can hide conflict. Two notes may receive the same number of new ratings, but one may gain broad approval while another gains approval from allies and rejection from opponents. The method improves on the naive view by measuring the composition and direction of new evidence, not just its amount.
424.po: The payoff is a clearer diagnosis of a real weakness in consensus-based fact-checking. The platform's bridging-based algorithm may select helpful notes at the moment of display, but the paper shows that this state is not final. In the studied data, 30.2% of displayed notes later lose helpful status and disappear. The practical capability is early warning: if post-display rating volume and viewpoint-specific leaning reveal polarization, designers can see when visibility is destabilizing consensus rather than confirming it, and treat that phase as part of the system.
424.limits: The abstract supports strong evidence about observed rating dynamics, but it does not prove every reason a person rated a note. Viewpoint similarity to the note author is a useful signal, not a full description of belief, motivation, coordination, or attention. The counterfactual results depend on the modeling choices and on whether the measured data captures the main causes of disappearance. The findings also come from Community Notes on X, so other fact-checking systems may differ if their contributor pools, display rules, or rating incentives differ.

425.bp: Factories, wind farms, power plants, and other industrial sites depend on machines that rarely fail without warning. Bearings heat up, vibration changes, pressure drifts, and many sensors report those small changes before a breakdown becomes visible. Predictive maintenance tries to turn that continuous sensor flow into early warnings so people can repair equipment before downtime, safety risk, or replacement cost grows. The difficulty is that the warning must be fast and understandable. A plant operator cannot wait for every reading to travel to a distant cloud system before deciding whether a machine is safe. At the same time, an unexplained alert is not enough, because maintenance staff need to know which signals changed and what kind of failure the pattern resembles. ECLAD serves this operating need: it treats anomaly detection as a live industrial workflow where fast local screening, stronger remote checking, and human-readable diagnosis must cooperate.
425.wh: The hard part is a three-way tension between speed, accuracy, and explanation. Modern machinery produces many sensor channels at once, so the system is not judging one temperature value in isolation. It is judging whether a moving pattern across vibration, pressure, temperature, and other readings still looks like normal operation. Sending all of that data to the cloud can give access to larger models, but it costs bandwidth and adds delay. Keeping everything on the edge device, meaning the computer close to the machine, gives quick answers but limits model size and reasoning depth. A second difficulty is that sensor anomalies are not automatically maintenance diagnoses. A spike may be sensor noise, a short operating transition, or a sign of a real fault. The system therefore has to avoid both missed failures and noisy false alarms, while also producing an explanation that a human can inspect rather than a bare alarm label.
425.naive: A smart beginner might put one anomaly detector beside the machine and fire an alert whenever any sensor crosses a fixed threshold or looks unusual compared with recent history. That is attractive because it is fast and cheap. It fails because industrial signals are multivariate: several readings may be harmless alone but suspicious together, and one large value may be normal during a known operating phase. Another beginner move is to upload everything to a cloud model. That gives more computing power, but the abstract says cloud-centered solutions suffer from bandwidth and latency limits. A third shortcut is to ask a language model to explain alerts after the fact. That can produce fluent text, but without verified evidence and a maintained anomaly taxonomy, the explanation may be a story rather than a useful diagnostic report.
425.ap: ECLAD's central move is to split the work by where each part is strongest. The edge device does the first pass. It runs a lightweight screen over the incoming sensor stream so obvious or urgent unusual patterns can be caught without waiting for remote computation. Cases that need deeper judgment are then passed to the cloud, where a higher-capacity sequence model can examine the ordered sensor history more carefully. Sequence model here means a model built to use order: what happened before changes the meaning of what happens now. After the cloud verification step, language-model-based interpretability agents turn the detected anomaly into a natural-language diagnostic report and update a self-evolving anomaly classification tree. That tree is a growing set of named anomaly categories, so explanations do not remain one-off paragraphs; they become part of an organized memory of fault types.
425.mech: The input is a live stream of multivariate sensor readings from industrial machinery. Multivariate means several measured channels arrive together, so the system sees a pattern across channels and time rather than a single number. First, the edge component watches this stream close to the machine. Its job is screening: keep the response time low, identify readings or short windows that look suspicious, and avoid sending every ordinary moment across the network. Second, when the edge screen finds a possible anomaly, the relevant sensor segment is sent to the cloud. The cloud component uses a higher-capacity sequence model, meaning a model with more computing room to compare the current ordered pattern with longer or richer histories. It verifies whether the edge warning is likely to be a true anomaly rather than noise. Third, if the event is verified, interpretability agents based on a language model examine the anomaly evidence and generate a diagnostic report in ordinary language. Fourth, the system maintains a self-evolving anomaly classification tree. A tree is a hierarchy: broad abnormal categories can split into more specific ones as new cases are seen. The output is therefore not just yes or no. It is a timely alert, a verified anomaly judgment, an explanatory report, and a browsable category structure shown through a web interface for time-series exploration and anomaly category browsing.
425.math: The mathematical ideas are sequence comparison, anomaly scoring, resource allocation, and hierarchical classification. Sequence comparison starts from the fact that sensor readings have order. A pressure rise after a temperature rise may mean something different from the same values in the opposite order, so the system needs memory of recent steps rather than a bag of measurements. Anomaly scoring means defining what normal sensor behavior looks like from repeated operation, then measuring how surprising a new pattern is. The score is useful only if it balances sensitivity against false alarms: too strict misses early failures, too loose interrupts operators with noise. Resource allocation enters through the edge-cloud split. The scarce resources are time, bandwidth, and computing power, so the system spends cheap local computation on many cases and expensive cloud computation on selected cases. The classification tree adds a structured counting-and-naming idea. Similar anomalies should be grouped under shared categories, while truly different fault patterns should branch apart. The language model, a text system trained to produce and interpret natural language, is used for explanation, but the math still depends on keeping sensor evidence, sequence judgment, and category structure tied together.
425.dots: This paper sits in the anomaly detection family because it asks when a case stops fitting expected behavior. It connects directly to the time-series and spatiotemporal family, where the core problem is preserving order, rhythm, drift, and sudden shocks in streams before making a forecast or warning. It also belongs with interpretability work: the abstract does not treat an alert as complete unless the system can produce a natural-language diagnostic report and organize anomaly categories for browsing. The edge-cloud design links it to efficiency and systems papers, where the question is which work should happen near the data and which work deserves more remote computation. Neighboring ideas include probability, because verification is about estimating whether a suspicious pattern is plausible or truly abnormal; sequence modeling, because the order of sensor changes matters; and language-model agents, because the final step turns technical evidence into a report that maintenance users can inspect.
425.ww: The design should work better than a single local or cloud-only detector because it matches each stage to a different failure mode. Edge screening handles the fact that industrial alerts need immediacy. It can catch suspicious moments without waiting for a network round trip and without paying to move every normal reading. Cloud verification handles the edge device's weakness: a small local screen may be fast but may not have enough capacity to distinguish noise from a real multi-sensor pattern. A stronger sequence model can recheck the ordered evidence with more context. The language-model explanation layer handles a different weakness again. Even a correct anomaly score does not tell a technician what changed, how to categorize the event, or what related cases have appeared before. The evolving classification tree gives the reports a memory structure, so new anomalies can refine the category system instead of disappearing as isolated incidents. The approach therefore reduces overload at the cloud, preserves quick response at the machine, and gives humans an inspectable account of the alert.
425.po: The payoff is an end-to-end maintenance system rather than only an anomaly score. According to the abstract, ECLAD preserves real-time responsiveness at the edge while using cloud resources for higher-precision and interpretable analysis. It also demonstrates the system through a web-based interface where users can explore time-series behavior and browse anomaly categories. For maintenance teams, that means a possible route from raw sensor streams to a verified warning, then to a readable diagnostic report and a growing anomaly taxonomy. The practical gain is faster triage with more context: operators can see not only that the machine looked abnormal, but also how the system classified and explained the abnormal pattern.
425.limits: The claims depend on the edge screen catching the right candidate events. If the lightweight stage misses a subtle early fault, the cloud verifier never sees it. If it sends too many doubtful segments, bandwidth and latency pressures return. The cloud sequence model also assumes past sensor histories contain patterns that separate real faults from harmless operating changes. The language-model agents assume the evidence supplied to them is reliable enough to explain; the abstract does not prove that every report is faithful to the detector's actual reasoning. The evolving anomaly tree is useful only if new categories are placed correctly. The abstract reports an end-to-end demonstration and available code, but not full deployment evidence across machines, factories, sensor failures, or changing maintenance procedures.

426.bp: Many real-world datasets are structured as graphs—social networks, citation webs, knowledge bases—where each node (a person, a paper, a concept) has text attached. Training a full neural network and language model jointly on million-node graphs is slow and wasteful. The goal is to compress the graph down to tiny synthetic version that trains equally well, saving energy and time.
426.wh: Most graph compression methods ignore the text. They compress only the structure (the connections). But text-attributed graphs are twice as hard: you must compress both the text descriptions and the topology while preserving what the joint model learns. Text compression is novel to this problem. Also, existing compression methods that match training trajectories (the path of improving accuracy during training) suffer from high variance—different random seeds produce wildly different compressed graphs.
426.ap: TAGSAM uses two parallel strategies. For text: it selects representative chunks from descriptions of related nodes and merges them, picking chunks that carry maximum information (information maximization). For graph structure: instead of directly matching training trajectories, it aligns similarity matrices—stable representations of which nodes are 'close'—avoiding the high variance of trajectory matching.
426.ww: The two-part design respects the dual nature of the problem. Text selection via mutual information maximization keeps only the unique signal from descriptions. The similarity-matrix matching is more stable because it focuses on static structural relationships rather than the noisy trajectory of training. Together, they preserve what the model actually uses: semantic content and relational structure.
426.po: On CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, TAGSAM compresses graphs to 1% of original size with only 4.9% accuracy loss compared to the best competitor. The method generalizes across different neural architectures and languages, making the compressed dataset truly reusable instead of model-specific.

427.bp: News travels fast online, but spotting trends early is harder than you'd think. Trending detection usually waits for people to search—'what's everyone looking for?'—but by the time search volume rises, millions have already missed the story. In low-traffic contexts (rare or long-tail topics), there's no search signal at all. The goal is to predict what will trend before anyone searches.
427.wh: The cold-start problem is real: without search queries, you have no signal. News posts and posts arrive constantly, but they sit invisible until search volume emerges, and by then it's stale. Keyword frequency in posts is slow and fragile. You need a way to simulate search queries from posts themselves, then score which synthetic queries will matter. But language models drift over time—what seemed important last week might not be important this week.
427.ap: RTTP generates search queries directly from news content using a continual-learning language model. It scores each synthetic query by combining engagement strength (how many likes/shares/comments) with creator authority (how influential is the person posting). As new content arrives and trends shift, the model retrains continuously. But continuous retraining risks 'catastrophic forgetting'—the model forgets how to generate good queries from earlier patterns. So the authors propose Mix-Policy DPO, a preference learning technique that blends on-policy training (keeping what worked) with off-policy exploration (discovering new patterns).
427.ww: By generating synthetic search queries, you're creating signal where none existed. The engagement + authority scoring prioritizes content that matters socially, not just what's being discussed. Continual learning lets the model adapt weekly. Mix-Policy DPO keeps the model stable (remembering what worked) while allowing evolution (learning new trends), avoiding the oscillation or collapse that usually happens with naive retraining.
427.po: Deployed at Facebook and Meta, RTTP achieves 91.4% improvement in tail-trend detection precision and 19% better query generation accuracy than baselines. The system sustains stable performance through multi-week online retraining, turning latent signals in content into early-warning trend predictions.

428.bp: Video captioning—automatically writing a sentence or two describing a video—sounds simple but is hard because you must understand both visual motion and semantic meaning, then align them into coherent language. A caption must match the video's action and significance. Getting this right matters for search, accessibility, and video understanding systems.
428.wh: Most methods focus on extracting visual features (objects, motion) but treat language as an afterthought. They ignore the rich semantic links between what you see and what words mean. A video of 'a person running in a park' could be tagged 'exercise', 'outdoor activity', or 'jogging', but which fits best requires understanding how visual concepts and language concepts relate. Naive methods miss these cross-modal relationships.
428.ap: MGCDVc uses two ideas together: a graph-based semantic model and a diffusion-based generation model. It creates latent 'concept anchors'—abstract bridges between visual features and language—then builds a weighted graph connecting visual nodes, textual nodes, and anchors. It then generates the caption by working through this graph structure, where each word-node and its connections are revealed gradually, like diffusion filling in a picture pixel by pixel. A soft pruning mechanism removes low-quality nodes, cleaning up the graph.
428.ww: Graphs capture relationships: which visual elements relate to which concepts, which words co-occur naturally. Diffusion-based generation respects these relationships gradually instead of predicting all words at once. This structured generation is more coherent because each new word is aware of the graph context, not just previous words. Pruning keeps the reasoning lean by discarding noisy, unhelpful nodes.
428.po: On standard benchmarks, MGCDVc improves caption accuracy and relevance by incorporating relational reasoning. The graph-conditioned diffusion approach produces more semantically coherent captions than methods that treat visual and language features independently, especially on complex scenes with multiple actions.

429.bp: Cryptocurrencies like Ethereum host decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms where users lend and borrow money recorded as immutable on-chain transactions. These platforms are a rich source of temporal data: when do users deposit? When do they withdraw? When do defaults (non-payment) happen? Understanding these patterns—predicting who will churn or default—is crucial for platform stability. The field needs rigorous benchmarks to measure progress.
429.wh: Temporal prediction on Web3 is different from typical prediction: the data is public but sparse, transactions are recorded with exact timestamps but users' true intent is hidden, and the system evolves rapidly as new features arrive. Traditional benchmarks from web analytics don't capture this mix of sparsity, real-world censoring (some users disappear; you don't know if they quit or just went dormant), and non-stationarity (the system's behavior changes over time as adoption grows).
429.ap: The FinSurvival Challenge 2025 analyzed 21.8 million transactions from Aave v3, a major lending protocol. It defined 16 survival-prediction tasks: given a user's early activity, predict whether they'll still be active later (or default, or reduce activity). Winning solutions built domain-aware features—things like 'collateral volatility' and 'historical interest-rate sensitivity'—that generic time-series methods miss. The challenge published the dataset and evaluated reproducible results.
429.ww: Domain-aware features work because they encode the specific risks and incentives in DeFi: users care about collateral safety, interest rates matter differently than in traditional finance, and transaction costs drive behavior. A system agnostic to these realities—just looking at 'time since deposit'—misses key signals. The benchmark enforced reproducibility, spotting which methods generalize and which overfit.
429.po: The benchmark surfaces that temporal feature engineering (understanding DeFi mechanics) beats generic time-series models. This provides a foundation for measuring progress on Web3 prediction and a sandbox for testing techniques relevant to broader temporal analytics—churn, risk, evolution—that appear everywhere online.

430.bp: Planning a trip is tedious: you search blogs, articles, and reviews, then manually stitch together an itinerary day by day. The dream is an interactive tool that generates itineraries on the fly by reading current travel content and adapting to your preferences. A smart, controllable travel assistant would save hours.
430.wh: Travel blogs and articles are scattered, unstructured, and constantly changing. Each one covers different attractions with different depths. Extracting a coherent itinerary requires: fetching fresh content, distilling key attractions, reasoning about logistics (travel time between sites, opening hours), and ranking by user interest. No single off-the-shelf tool handles all steps, and cloud APIs are slow for interactive use.
430.ap: Roamify is a browser extension that runs end-to-end on your computer without hitting external servers. It scrapes current travel blogs, summarizes them using a finetuned T5 model to extract key attractions and descriptions, then generates a multi-day itinerary using LLaMA 3 language model. The user controls sliders encoding preferences: historical sites, natural parks, cultural landmarks, amusement parks. The LLM uses these sliders to rank and sequence attractions into a coherent plan.
430.ww: Client-side processing is crucial: no round-trip to a server, so responses feel instant. Finetuned summarization keeps extraction fast and domain-focused. Preference sliders make the system controllable—instead of a generic itinerary, you get one tuned to your interests. The language model acts as a reasoning engine, avoiding rigid rules ('do cultural sites before museums') and adapting to the actual content available.
430.po: Roamify demonstrates a complete pipeline: live data retrieval, neural summarization, preference modeling, and on-device language model inference. Users get interactive, up-to-date itineraries in seconds, with transparency (no cloud uploads) and control (sliders adjust recommendations), showcasing how language models can power real-time web intelligence applications.

431.bp: Detecting large-scale cyberattacks—a 'super host' sending traffic to thousands of distinct targets, or a victim host flooded by thousands of sources—is vital for network defense. ISPs and defenders use high-speed sketches (compact data structures that track patterns in data streams) to spot these threats without storing all traffic. The challenge is doing this accurately on real-world data with limited memory.
431.wh: Existing sketch-based approaches count distinct IP addresses as the sole signal of a super host. But attackers and botnets are smarter: they often communicate within the same subnet (the same geographic block of IP addresses, like 192.168.1.x). A naive 'distinct IP count' gives false positives—multiple hosts on one subnet look like one super host—and misses concentrated attacks within a subnet. Fixing this with hierarchical structures wastes memory.
431.ap: SegSketch introduces a 'halved-segment hashing' strategy that estimates the common prefix length of IP addresses without storing full addresses. Common prefixes reveal subnet relationships cheaply. The algorithm estimates cardinality (distinct count) within subnets, not across all addresses. This hybrid approach keeps memory low while capturing subnet-aware signals that naive full-address counting misses.
431.ww: The core insight is that attackers cluster geographically in IP space. By detecting that cluster structure—noticing that thousands of targets share a common subnet prefix—you identify real attacks, not noise. Halved-segment hashing efficiently infers prefix lengths without storing full IPs, so you get subnet awareness at sketch-level memory cost.
431.po: Real-world traces show SegSketch improves F1-score (a balance between false positives and false negatives) by up to 8x over state-of-the-art solutions, especially on tight memory budgets. This means network defenders can spot super hosts more reliably, reducing false alarms while catching real attacks.

432.bp: Social networks and online communities are structured as graphs of people and connections, often with text (posts, profiles). Detecting misinformation, toxic behavior, or other harms requires analyzing this graph. Large language models show promise for reasoning over such graphs, but you need labeled examples to teach them. Obtaining expert labels for sensitive content—'is this post misinformation?'—is slow, costly, and often impossible at scale.
432.wh: Instruction tuning, the standard way to adapt language models to graph tasks, requires many (INSTRUCTION, OUTPUT) pairs from labeled nodes. In social networks, labels are scarce: experts can label a few hundred posts, but the graph has millions. Standard methods ignore unlabeled nodes despite their relational structure. Labeled and unlabeled nodes are connected, and those connections carry signal, but naive supervised learning throws that signal away.
432.ap: SIT-Graph uses self-training: the model is initially finetuned on scarce labeled data, then iteratively improved by having it label unlabeled nodes and retraining on its own predictions (carefully, to avoid error accumulation). The key novelty is that instruction tuning (crafting task-specific prompts) is maintained throughout, not just at initialization. The method is model-agnostic; it works with any graph instruction-tuning approach.
432.ww: Self-training exploits the structure: if two unlabeled nodes are connected and one is mislabeled, nearby nodes' correct labels will eventually pull the model back. By carefully iterating—the model labels high-confidence examples, gets retrained, and refines its understanding—you bootstrap from few labels to strong performance. Maintaining instruction tuning throughout keeps the model reasoning in natural language, more interpretable than black-box features.
432.po: SIT-Graph reduces the need for labeled data while leveraging the full graph structure, making it practical to deploy LLMs on social networks for moderation and misinformation detection despite annotation scarcity. The self-training approach sustains performance across iterations, enabling sensitive applications where expert labels are limited.

433.bp: NFTs (non-fungible tokens) are digital assets—art, collectibles, virtual real estate—stored on blockchains. Their value proposition is permanence and decentralization: because they're on an immutable blockchain, you own them forever and can't be censored. But this promise depends on where the actual content lives. If the image or metadata is stored on a centralized server, that server can disappear, taking your asset with it.
433.wh: The inconvenient truth: most NFTs store actual content (images, videos) off-chain on servers like Amazon S3 or IPFS gateways operated by a single entity. The blockchain stores only a link—a pointer—to that content. If the server goes down, the link is worthless and your 'permanent' digital art is gone. High-value NFTs are often stored this way because blockchain storage is expensive, creating a 'Blue-chip Trap': the most valuable assets are the most fragile.
433.ap: The authors collected 16 million real NFTs and systematically audited their storage. They traced where each asset's content actually sits: centralized servers, fragile IPFS nodes, or truly decentralized systems. They found eight distinct vulnerabilities: access failures (server down), tamperability (server owner modifies content), and forgeability (attacker replaces content with a fake). They mapped real assets to this taxonomy and scored severity using CVSS (the industry standard for security vulnerability severity).
433.ww: The mismatch between promise and reality exposes a fundamental tension: immutability and decentralization are expensive at scale, so the industry took shortcuts. A blockchain transaction costs pennies but storing a megabyte of image data costs dollars, so builders stored only pointers. This works until the pointer breaks. The analysis shows these aren't theoretical risks—they're widespread, measurable defects affecting millions of high-value assets.
433.po: The taxonomy reveals eight classes of storage defects with severity scores. All pose substantial risks. The findings give developers concrete guidance on secure storage: use truly decentralized systems or redundancy, not single centralized servers. For users, it's a cautionary tale: 'permanent' NFTs aren't always permanent, and the most valuable ones are often the most at-risk.

434.bp: Ads and tracking scripts follow you across the web, profiling your behavior and serving targeted ads. Blocking them protects privacy and cuts bloat. Adblocker extensions detect and filter these scripts. But as ad networks evolve to evade blockers—obfuscating code, changing domain names, using new delivery methods—static filter lists fall behind. A smarter, learned system that adapts to evasion would be more resilient.
434.wh: Current machine learning ad blockers use features easily evaded by attackers: if the model learns 'URLs with pattern X are ads', attackers simply avoid pattern X. Adversarial attacks can fool detectors with small perturbations: changing a few characters in code or slightly modifying a domain name breaks detection (57-92% evasion rates reported). Also, models trained on one site's ads generalize poorly to others, and accuracy degrades over time as new ad techniques emerge, requiring expensive retraining.
434.ap: AdVersa uses hard-to-perturb features: embeddings from code (the actual script content) and URLs that capture deep semantic meaning, not surface patterns. The model is trained on a large 2.74M-request dataset and deployed on the client side (in your browser), never calling home. A pseudo-labeling strategy lets the model improve continuously on new traffic without manual retraining: it labels high-confidence new examples, learns from them, and adapts.
434.ww: Code and URL embeddings extract semantic patterns that survive minor perturbations. An attacker must rewrite logic or change domains substantially to evade, not just tweak surface text. Client-side deployment means the model sees and adapts to real traffic in real time. Pseudo-labeling reduces drift without annotation overhead—the model bootstraps corrections from its own confident predictions.
434.po: AdVersa achieves 98.23% F1 score, twice the robustness against adversarial attacks compared to baselines, and strong cross-domain generalization (91.47% F1 on unseen sites). Maintenance overhead drops by 99.8% through pseudo-labeling, eliminating the burden of curating filter lists or retraining. The lightweight client-side design protects privacy while delivering state-of-the-art blocking.
